skip_reason: Outbound collections and damage-claim call on a move that has already been performed, not a new-business sales conversation. Khevan states the purpose at the top — 'we've been playing a little bit of a phone tag here trying to get the payment. Get it all on the same page as far as the payment goes' — and the call is about an invoice that failed to capture on-site ('when they did it the first day it just timed out or the iPad kinda didn't work'), a billing correction he made himself ('I realized that the number was $5 too high cause I had inappropriately applied the discount for Willy'), a damage claim on furniture the crew scratched, and a courtesy return visit. The one forward-looking item — picking up leftover garage and patio items the truck could not fit — is overflow from the job already sold, not a new lead, and Khevan quotes no rate, gives no estimate, runs no intake and makes no booking. Per the brief's strict skip rule, a call that is mostly about an existing booked job is a skip even where a little pricing gets discussed. The 85-point sales scorecard does not apply and this call should not count toward the sales grading average.
top_strength: Unscored, but this is an unusually well-handled collections call and worth flagging to Carly as a claims-recovery example. The customer is 88, exhausted, half-blind, hard of hearing, mid-medical-crisis and sitting on a damage claim she is upset about — and Khevan never once pushed for the money. He took the pressure off explicitly and repeatedly: 'we're not gonna start sending you threatening emails or, or applying any sort of fees or anything like that' and later 'we've had invoices in the, in the nether for far longer than one week. So I'm not too concerned with you know, getting this sorted right this minute we have we can work with you on time, I'm not worried.' He proactively owned the billing confusion she was complaining about rather than defending it, naming his own error on the $5 discrepancy and the power-loss issue that stripped her signature from the contract. Best move of the call: he converted her damage complaint into a service action she had not asked for, at no charge — 'I would be happy as a courtesy to have a crew come and look at the dresser and submit the damage claim for you... I wouldn't charge you for the time that they're over there.' He was also straight on limits without being cold, giving the reason rather than just the no: 'we generally don't enter attics for liability reasons. So, while we could take the items we wouldn't be able to bring them down,' and the same on the gas mower. She ended the call volunteering thanks: 'I do, thank you for calling back and for being patient with my phone.'
coaching_note: Not scored on the sales rubric, but there is one concrete, coachable moment. The customer had to stop him: 'Kevin hasn't, Kevin among other things, I don't hear. Well and when you talk fast, I don't understand what you're saying anybody. I have to tell everybody this so you can just slow down a little bit.' He recovered well and restated it. But she had already told him early on that she was barely functioning, and he then spent several turns trying to spell his surname to a customer with a stated hearing problem — plain letters, then 'delta uniform? Echo, Charlie, kilo' — until she gave up entirely: 'I'm sorry. Forget it, just forget it.' Pace and abandoning a low-value thread are the two habits to work on. Separately, a process flag rather than a rep flag: an unsigned contract, a payment that never captured, twelve conflicting emails ('none of them made any sense. They were all, they all say something different'), a truck too small for the load, and undetected damage discovered days later all landed on one elderly customer from a single job. That combination is worth pulling the job record on, and the billing-email cadence is worth reviewing with Matisen — the customer's confusion here was manufactured by the system, not by her.
phone_presence_notes: Consistently warm and genuinely unhurried across 28 minutes of a difficult, rambling call — heavy use of 'No worries' and 'Of course,' real empathy framing ('our main goal is to, you know, alleviate some of the stress of moving'), and he let her tell the story about her late husband's 1962 furniture without steering her back to the invoice; held short of 5 because the customer explicitly called out his pace and he never adopted her name after she used his repeatedly.
audio_review_reason: The customer directly flagged a delivery problem — 'when you talk fast, I don't understand what you're saying' — which is exactly the kind of finding that can only be verified in audio, not transcript. Worth a listen to confirm whether he actually slowed down and held the slower pace for the rest of the call, since this was the single clearest coachable behavior in the file.
